newsitem.title: FRANCE: French deficit toll to be revaled by July 21 audit.
newsitem.headline: French deficit toll to be revaled by July 21 audit.

text.p: French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Tuesday an audit of public finances called for by the new left-wing government was likely to show that the previous government had worsened the public deficit this year.
But he said Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's government would balance any spending commitments by foregoing other expenditure it would otherwise like to have undertaken.

"Everything points to the budget, which you voted, not being fulfilled...The prime minister said the situation was serious, and it is," Strauss-Kahn told politicians from the previous centre-right government in the National Assembly.

"During the election campaign we promised not to worsen the deficit, but, unfortunately it has, because of your own decisions in the first half of the year," he said. "And the audit, I fear will reveal it."
"As a result the spending that we want to undertake will be weighted against a certain number of spending commitments that we will not make. This reflects our priorities," he said.
Strauss-Kahn said the audit of public finances commissioned by Jospin would be presented by its authors on July 21.
"It goes without saying that this report will be made public immediately."

Struass-Kahn said "it would be wise" for the opposition in parliament to hold its fire until the audit was completed and that there would be ample time to discuss the consequences when the next budget law was presented after the summer recess.

Strauss-Kahn's remarks to parliament came the same day as Bank of France governor told a news conference on the central bank's annual report that cutting the deficit was the key to boosting French growth.

There has been intense press speculation before and after the June 1 election which swept the left to power that France's public deficit this year -- the test year for the euro single currency -- could markedly overshoot the three percent of gross domestic product dictated by a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty.
The new French government has committed itself to joining the single currency on time in 1999 but says there should be a flexible reading of the Maastricht treaty economic fitness criteria.
